utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know if Your Honours have had a chance to look at the summary for the next witness. If so, the Court will see on the last paragraph, although there's no written application in, there is an application for limited protection. I can deal with it at the moment without even going into private session, so that as much as possible of our proceedings may be public. This is a witness who gives, in a sense, quite limited evidence. He's necessary because he's the only witness of one particular village, and therefore he has to be here, but his evidence is otherwise non-specific in relation to either defendant. He's an intelligent, educated man, and he recognizes those characteristics of his own evidence, and he's not in any sense anxious to ask for protection. But of course, once witnesses come here, they have to be told of the potential for applications for protection. It will come as no surprise to you to know that, so far as I'm concerned, they then receive the maximum encouragement possible to give evidence fully publicly, for I would prefer it that those who have the courage and confidence to do so can do so. But for the reasons set out in the last two lines, or two and a half lines, of paragraph 19, which are made not on his own behalf but for someone else, he expresses, I dare say, an understandable anxiety. And it's all very easy for me to be bold and to press people to take what they would believe to be risks. He asks, respectfully, that he may have that protection, and I happily, in the circumstances, make that application on his behalf. The person concerned is -- well, you see the age set out there, and as you'll discover from the rest of the narrative, was with him throughout the events that he speaks of. This wasn't a case of separated families; this was families kept together in the comparatively unpleasant circumstances in which they found themselves, and I think that the person identified there was, as is so often the case, concerned for the relation who comes here to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll hear from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence of Mr. Kordic does not object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Neither do we, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll make the order as asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, then, may the Chamber be prepared for his arrival. The witness will become witness --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: -- AJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. While these administrative things are being done, and so as not to waste time, can I bring you up to date with a couple things. Negotiations have gone on this morning with Mr. Lopez-Terres and counsel for both defendants in relation to the map. Mr. Lopez-Terres will be able to tell you later what progress, if any, has been made. It sounds, from what I've heard, to be rather -- perhaps somewhat limited, but we're certainly hoping to call the map-maker tomorrow, and matters not agreed can be dealt with in the conventional way then. Can I revert briefly to the tape. The Chamber will remember that some uncertainties about transcription led to the Chamber admitting the majority of the tape but for the time being not admitting or not attending to the balance. The Chamber knows, and I think the Defence knows, that we are, of course, obliged to use, and in a sense to count as authoritative, the official translation services of our institution which serves all parts of the institution. Sometimes it's possible to improve on what they can hear, perhaps by taking more time than they have or using better equipment and so on, and we've been able to provide a fuller transcription of the tape, indeed in one or two passages. One passage, I think, where the official transcribers marked the tape as inaudible, it is possible, by taking time, to make out, I think, some 20 lines -- I'm not sure -- of further conversation. That's been done, and the additional transcriptions have been distributed to the Defence some days ago, I think, now. It's also possible, so far as we are concerned, to be quite satisfied that both tapes, the one that the witness himself produced and the one that had been produced by him earlier and brought here via investigators and lawyers, are identical, save, I think, for the bips or knocking sounds that are on them. So I think it will be possible to agree the revised transcript, subject the bipping noises, and I have got those revised transcripts for production to the Chamber at some stage today.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with respect to the tape, I would be more than happy to explain the Defence's position once the witness has testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If the witness would take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you've been granted protection by the Judges, which means that your name will not be given and your face will not be shown. Can you, therefore, look at this piece of paper, and without reading the name on it, simply say yes if it is your name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You will be known in these proceedings as Witness AJ. Witness AJ, did you graduate as an economist, living in Ilidza, which is close to Sarajevo, until first compelled in April of 1992 to move to Hadzici, which happened to be the place where the electricity company you worked for was based?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Forced to move by, as you described them, I think, the Chetniks, you moved with your wife and child, and you moved to Mount Bjelasnica and, indeed, specifically, to the village of Kramari.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That shortly after that, you moved to Kiseljak, in May 1992, living first in the house of a colleague of yours in Behrici. On the ELMO is a map, the number of which is 1891.1, but I've turned down the label so that we can fit as much of it as possible onto the overheard projector. If you could use the pointer that you'll find there and just show us where the village of Behrici is, and maybe the technical staff can focus in on it a little bit for us, because it's -- you may want to find Kiseljak first and then show us the village to which you moved in May of 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. At that stage, were you in a position to judge the degree to which Croats and Serbs were able to travel between Kiseljak and Ilidza, and I suppose Sarajevo, but maybe not, but certainly between Kiseljak and Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes. There was regular city transport that provided services daily, several times a day, in fact, from Kiseljak to Ilidza, and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that transport only used by Croats and Serbs, or was it available to and used by Muslims as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: No, Muslims could not use that transport. It was only used by Croats and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because you had by then been forced out of the place where you originally had lived.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: We moved to a village called Hercezi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'll come to that in a second. Before we do, in the middle of 1992, did the HVO take over control of aspects of daily life in the Kiseljak municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In particular, just give us a list, if you can, of the things they took over.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Well, in the Kiseljak command, before they took over the power, that building was shared by the TO and the HVO. However, subsequently, when they took over the power, the BH Army had to move to a village called Gomionica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: They also took over the control over the power distribution system in so-called Herceg-Bosna, that is, the sub-transformer station at Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether they took over other aspects of political administration in the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes, they took over all political power.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you moved in the middle of, or slightly after the middle of 1992 to which village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: The name of the village is Hercezi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we see that, please, on the map, just so that we can have an idea of where that is. Again, if the technical staff is able to get a closer focus on this map, it would be possibly helpful; but it may not be possible, and I understand that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just point out so that we can all see where Kiseljak is. It's just visible.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is north-west of Kiseljak. Roughly how many kilometres away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: The village is some five kilometres from Kiseljak, in the direction of Fojnica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were now in a house on your own, is this right, with your family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you still able to work for a time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes, for a time I could work, but then problems began to arise during that time, so that my ability to work was limited.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were working, where was that? Was that in Kiseljak or was that in Behrici, or where? Not Behrici. Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: No, not in Hadzici. The team employed in the maintenance of the power lines was at Kiseljak, and we would come to the subtransformer station at Kiseljak every day and then establish connection with Energoinvest in Sarajevo, who issued us work orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke of the HVO taking over the control of power lines. Did that have an effect on your employment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they take over your business, and did they ban you from going to work in due course?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The banning of your going to work was built on an accusation that you'd been taking diesel fuel; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So from that moment were you without work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: I was largely prevented from the job I had been assigned to do, but for a while I somehow managed in another way, almost right up to the breaking of the conflict between the HVO and the BH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was it that they took over the electricity business, according to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: It was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Middle, beginning, end? What?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: I'd say towards the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 18th of April of 1993, where were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: My family and I were in the house that we had been put up in in the village of Hercezi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: We heard detonations and gunfire. We woke up and saw that there was very fierce gunfire and detonations in the village of Gomionica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Gomionica is, as we can see on the map, but it's not showing up terribly well, Gomionica is the other side of the main road from Hercezi; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Beyond Gromiljak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes, beyond Gromiljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you leave your house and go to the lower part of the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes. All the Muslims who lived in that part of the village left the houses and withdrew to the lower part of the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you see of soldiers and, if so, what type of soldiers did you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: When we withdrew to the lower part of the village, I saw three or four soldiers wearing HVO or, rather, with HVO insignia, and they were patrolling the road that goes through the village, on one side. On the other, I saw two soldiers in identical uniforms and with identical patches, who were not patrolling, who were merely standing by with weapons in their hands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The following day, did a large number of people go pretty well due south to the village of Doci?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes. I think there were more than 200 people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That other small village, Doci, had that, to your knowledge, been disarmed to any extent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To what degree, to your knowledge, had it ever been armed in the first place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: One cannot speak about any major quantity of weapons. All I saw were a couple of hunting rifles and several pistols.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having got to the village, did you judge it safer to spend the night in the woods to which you fled?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And a day later, were you told by someone that the HVO was looking for you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes. I was told a man, Hikmet Turcinovic is his name, came to look for us in the wood and to tell me that they were looking for me and that I had to go back to the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do as ordered and return to Hercezi, to discover that the remaining villagers there had been disarmed, although the residents had not been mistreated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you report to the man in charge, Pero Vucic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes, I reported, and my name was taken down in a notebook of some sort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At about that time, possibly a little later, did you get the impression that they'd sought you out in particular, for a particular reason?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: In my opinion, they were looking for me, because the house I was staying in, I had a car there, and I think they wanted to take that car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, I think you'd already got rid of the car to someone else for the time being, so they didn't get it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes. They came. There were two men in HVO uniforms. One of them had a white soldier's belt, so I assumed he belonged to the police. They said that they had a report that there were weapons in that house, and then they demanded that I open the garage for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Passing from your own house and problems to what you saw of others, did you see other houses attacked at all by HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Several days later, I saw a house set on fire in that village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose house was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: I was not born in those parts, so I don't know the names, but I know the nickname of this person who had this house, and the nickname was Kuja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you now staying at the house of Safet Turcinovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to that house and what happened to you at the same time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: One night we heard a blow outside the house where the electricity installations were. First the electricity went off, and then they thumped on the door. I opened the door and an automatic rifle was pointed at me, and a lamp. I was just told to sit down and there would be no problems, and then two men entered the house and looted it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those two men, did you know who they were? Or the man who held you will at gunpoint, do you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: They had woolen hoods over their faces with openings for the eyes, so I didn't recognise them at that time, but the next day my daughter recognised one of them, who was carrying a stolen radio cassette recorder to sell it. They were brothers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And their names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Vinko Tuka is one of them. I don't remember the others. Vinko Tuka and his brother, also Tuka, is the surname.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you made your statement to the ICTY, were you able to remember the name then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that name Branko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's right; it was Branko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you confined in Hercezi from the 20th of April, for five or four and a half months, until the 6th of September?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: We continued to stay in those houses, and I consider that to have been a kind of house arrest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you required to report, I think initially twice a day and then subsequently daily, to the HVO headquarters in the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you and other men taken out by the HVO to do various jobs? I think one may have been clearing a road, cutting wood, and digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there only one occasion that you can tell us about when digging trenches was associated with danger; namely, when you were digging trenches by some BiH lines and there was some gunshots?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes. One morning an HVO soldier who lived in that same village and whose name I don't know -- I just know he used to be a taxi driver before the war -- he took us at gunpoint to dig trenches and make a dugout in the ground in a dangerous spot, where we could hear gunfire. Gunshots were fired above our heads, because opposite were the BiH front lines, and they fired above our heads, probably to prevent us from continuing to dig.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that apart, the treatment by the HVO in Hercezi was not too bad physically, although psychologically, obviously enough, life was difficult for you and your family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes. I had the good fortune not to have been exposed to physical abuse, but psychologically it was very hard. We didn't fear the locals who were members of the HVO, but occasionally other units would come to the village, wearing HVO uniforms, when we had to flee and go into hiding so as not to be captured by them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 6th of September of 1993, were you, with the other villagers, transferred to Rotilj, by now a detention camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the treatment at Rotilj compare with the treatment you'd had at Hercezi?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: It was worse in Rotilj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were people forced to go to front lines to dig trenches, to cut and transport wood, clear out garbage, and so on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you yourself ever go for forced work or were you able to in some way protect yourself from these risks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: I did go several times, but sometimes I did manage to avoid going, claiming sickness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there two men there from Visnjica, Sadik Turko -- I beg your pardon. Was there one man from Visnjica, Osman Sehic, and another man from Hercezi, Sadik Turko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did they behave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: I can say with certainty regarding Sadik Turko, because, personally, I didn't have much contact with Osman. Sadik Turko behaved as if he was working to get extra money the harder we worked, as if he was going to get more money out of it, and he forced us to work very hard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you heard of people being used as human shields at Gomionica, and you heard of people being beaten at the barracks; is that correct? Gomionica, sorry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: What I heard was the following: From the Rotilj camp, men and women were selected to be used as human shields, if necessary, at HVO lines behind Kresevo, in the direction of Tarcin, and from the camp in Kresevo, allegedly -- this is something I did not see -- people were to be used as human shields at Gomionica. Hikmet Turcinovic was taken to the barracks, and he was returned several days later, after having suffered many blows, and he was injured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did your detention at Rotilj end, and when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: We were exchanged through a so-called private channel at the end of November 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you wait there. You may be asked some further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I only have a few questions for this witness. Cross-examined by Mr. Naumovski:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness AJ, let me introduce myself. We can't see each other very well because of the ELMO, but never mind. My name is Mitko Naumovski, I'm an attorney from Zagreb, and together with Mr. Sayers, we represent Mr. Dario Kordic. I have several questions for you. Please bear in mind that these proceedings are being interpreted, so make a brief pause before answering my questions. Actually, I have two groups of questions for you, several linked to the village of Hercezi and several others to the village of Rotilj. If I understood you correctly, after the 18th of April, 1993, when you returned to the village, you heard that the village had been disarmed; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: No one had any weapons -- yes, you said I should wait. No one had any weapons in the village at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I read this from your statement which you gave to the Centre of Security Services in Sarajevo in November 1993. "They were disarmed, but there were very few weapons." That's what you said. So I inferred from that that you knew that there had been some weapons.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes. As far as the weapons are concerned, I have already said that I saw several hunting rifles and several pistols. But on the 18th of -- this was on the 18th of April, 1992, when we retreated to the lower part of the village. After that, I didn't see any weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you were thinking of 1993, but you said 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, of course. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it that you had no military duties, so you don't know much about military matters. But still let me ask you: You will agree that the local commander was Pero Vucic, called Madzar, as you said a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that local unit, there were only several HVO soldiers, locals.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes. All the people living there put on uniforms, but they were not many.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A moment ago you said that the local Croats who used to live in that village treated you relatively well; there were no particular problems with them at that time, were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes, there weren't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Problems were provoked by people from outside the village who came to loot; they were the ones who caused problems, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: I'm afraid you're not right. The people who looted the house I was staying in at the time came from that same village, whereas the people who came from outside were HVO troops, and they would capture men in the village and take them by truck to barracks. On one occasion, they took an elderly man -- I think he was among the oldest inhabitants of the village -- and they took him off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Actually, my question was, would you agree with me that the local people, Croats, assisted you Muslims in your day-to-day life? For example, Ruza Vucic, Vesna Pladic, and some other women of the village.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes. Ruza and Vesna did help us, but the others did not, and the local commander -- I don't know what military role he had. I think he was the local commander -- was quite correct in his treatment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we agree, Witness AJ, that the pressure on you, the inhabitants of that village, was particularly intensified when exiled Croats from Fojnica, Travnik, and other places began to arrive there in large numbers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes, one could say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that precisely due to that heightened pressure by people who were coming from places where they had been evicted and were moving into houses in your village, that that was the reason why you yourself had to move in 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: I do not agree with that statement. My opinion is that all of this was planned to happen in this way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But we did agree that thousands of refugees came to the area, especially from Fojnica, at the beginning of July 1993, and then from Travnik again in June 1993, and so on. We agree in that regard, don't we?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: I saw two or three families that fit the description you have given. I assume they came from Fojnica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A couple of questions about the village of Rotilj itself. People were living in houses, as is customary in villages, were they not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes. But the house I was staying in, which is a very, very small house, I think this was somebody's weekend home, and there were five families being accommodated there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, Witness AJ, that in the village of Rotilj, there was a kind of barrier at the entrance to the village, and there were several soldiers standing there? A sort of entrance barrier.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the village of Rotilj had no other fence around it, except for this obstacle at the entrance to the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: There was no need for any fences, as it is in a valley surrounded by hills -- I don't know their names -- and all these hills were under HVO control. So there was no where where we could go, nor where we would dare to go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness AJ, would you agree that, except for the guards at the entrance to the village, there were no HVO soldiers deployed in the village itself, inside the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Inside the village, not on a permanent basis. But as in the case of Hercezi, they would come occasionally and collect the men. In the village itself, it is true that there were no soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that regular medical aid was provided in the village, because every Tuesday, at 10 in the morning, there was a kind of surgery where a doctor called Lovric and a nurse called Iva Topic would come to treat patients?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: I didn't see that, but I did hear that they came, but only once. Hikmet Turcinovic, whom I have already mentioned, when he was beaten up, was taken to the hospital in Kiseljak, as there was no medical treatment available in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But this was not a permanent clinic; this was just occasional visits by the doctor.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: I have already answered your question. I said that I hadn't seen it, but I had heard that they had come once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. There was also a labour squad in Rotilj, as you told us a moment ago, a labour unit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned today Sadik Turko and Osman Sehic, who behaved like brigade leaders towards you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: I am quite sure that there were two of them. Sadik Turko is one of them. I had little contact with the other one. I assumed that it was Osman Sehic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But will you agree with me that those two persons are Muslim by ethnicity and religion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that humanitarian aid was distributed by Caritas in the village, flour and other foods?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes. Two or three times, I saw them from a distance when they were distributing aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour. Thank you, Witness AJ. Cross-examined by Mr. Mikulicic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness AJ. I am attorney Mikulicic, and together with my colleague, Kovacic, we represent the second accused, Mario Cerkez. Witness AJ, at the time that we have been discussing, you were working in the power distribution company, were you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: I was employed in Energoinvest. That is another company. It is not the electricity distribution office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you worked for a time in Kiseljak, where the main transformer station was, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes. But I didn't work in the transformer station itself. I had permission to establish contact with my firm in Sarajevo through that transformer station, to discuss work with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, where did the electricity go to from that transformer station? To which parts of Bosnia did it supply power?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: I have already told you that I am not, nor did I work in the transformer station. But as far as I'm familiar with the power system, it was all interconnected, and it could have gone in various directions, including Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you cannot tell us anything more about that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: No. Our team was working on the repair of power pillars and high-voltage installations. I'm an economist by profession, and I was not directly involved in those activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that case, I have no further questions for you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have just three more questions, please. Re-examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When, in Hercezi, outside HVO came to take men, what was the attitude of the local HVO? Did they try to protect you, did they let them in, or was it done without their knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: No one protected us. I don't know whether they wanted to, but they did not protect us. We had to flee and to hide.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give an estimate of the number of men taken off in these circumstances during your detention in Hercezi?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: I cannot give you a precise number because I fled too. But I do know that an old man was taken away, whose surname is Turcinovic. I don't know his first name, but they called him Hadzija. That I know for a fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any more details of any other men taken, if there were more than one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: They took Hikmet Turcinovic from Hercezi as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, there seems to be a suggestion that there was a mass movement of people to Hercezi by plan. Had you gone there according to some larger plan? If not, how did you come to live there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't quite understand your question. Could you repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, how did you come to live in Hercezi? Was this according to some large plan that people should move to this village, or was it by some other means?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: I was living in Ilidza, near Sarajevo, from which we were chased out by the Chetniks. And by chance I went first to Hadzici, then from Hadzici to Bjelasnica, from Mount Bjelasnica to Kiseljak, to the village of Behrici, and I stayed with a colleague of mine from work; and then two or three months later to Hercezi, where they found an old, small house for us where we could stay alone as a family. So there was no plan on our part; we were simply chased out, and we had to move out and look for lodgings elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nothing else of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness AJ, thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give your evidence. Your evidence is concluded and you are released.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the Court to be reconstituted into full open session and while we're waiting for Mr. Lopez-Terres to join us for the next topic, it might be convenient to remember to hear from Mr. Sayers on the tapes so we know what the position is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, reporting in for Mr. Stein, who's handled the audio tape issues, Mr. Kordic's position is as follows, four real points, I gather: First, we don't have the original tape, as the Court knows. All we have is a copy, and the copy was apparently made from the copy. The second copy appears to be better than the first copy. There are bleeps on it which are completely unexplained, and we are uninformed -- we have no information as to why the tape quality on the OTP's second copy that we've been provided is better than the tape quality of the tape that the witness actually brought to the court. We don't know if sound filters were used. We're looking into that. With respect to conversations 10 and 11 on the first side of the original tape and conversations 1, 2, and 3 on the reverse side of that tape, apparently conversations 1 and 2 on side 2 are indistinguishable, and we just have no idea how the translators were able to distinguish them. With respect to conversation 11 on the first side of the tape, apparently it goes over to conversation number 1 on side 2 of the tape, and there's -- we've listened to the tape, we've listened diligently, and there are about 19, 20 lines of the conversation that are completely indistinguishable. So once again, we don't know how the translators were able to translate something that you can't even hear. We have no idea why there are differences in tape quality. Suffice it to say, we're still looking into that. We'll try to work with the Prosecution in reaching a definitive position with respect to the tape as soon as we can, and I'll report further in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know whether the Court is intending to take a break at some stage in this longer afternoon or not, but the next item on the agenda, I think, is dead and unwilling witnesses, and I'm quite happy to get started on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it's early for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. Can I, while we're waiting for Mr. Lopez-Terres, who's going to deal with one particular aspect of this, can I distribute a document that lists witnesses for the Chamber and my friends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is this the Prosecutor's argument?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, it's not an argument; it's just a list of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we've got a list. It's headed "Prosecutor's Argument."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've got that already. The Defence hasn't got it. I'm sorry, the Defence hasn't got it yet. Can I distribute that now. I didn't realise that hadn't gone over to the other side. While waiting, it might help if I just review the position right from the beginning of the trial. The position, as the Court will remember, is that we, of course, expected to have to call nearly all witnesses live. We were being, I think, invited by the Chamber, from an early stage, to consider affidavits. The inability of the Defence to agree on any matters in relation to villages led to the Tulica application and its decision, which was reflected in the decisions further made last week. Along the way, other problems have been identified and to a limited extent argued, and I've always proposed, and I think with justification, that it would be helpful to put off resolution of all outstanding matters until a near final or final position could be seen, and this little chart, I think, pretty well sets out the final position. There are two witnesses who would have given evidence had they not died. We're in open session, so I won't use any names for the time being, for obvious reasons. The first, witness number 1, is a witness who deals with events in Donja Veceriska generally and fully, and in particular with a sighting there of the defendant Kordic. He has made a statement. His statement was admitted in Blaskic at the request of the Defence, but we argue that he should be admitted in this case. Number 2 made a statement fuller, from the Kordic point of view, than his prior testimony. The Court has already ruled at a much earlier stage that the prior testimony could go in but that it would reserve its position in relation to the statement at the same time as it reserved its decision to the statement of number 1. I'll return to Category B at the end of things, because that's a slightly different category in various ways. Category 3 is those witnesses who, despite all endeavours by us and all proper coercive measures of the Chamber, remain unwilling to respond to subpoenas, or possibly, in the case of number 8, incapable, through ill-health, from attending before the projected conclusion of the Prosecution case. Those witnesses are names with which the Chamber and my friends -- at least, 5, 6, and 7 -- will be familiar. Number 8 may, I think, be comparatively new, it only recently coming to our attention that he was unavailable. Category D is new subpoenas required in respect of people whose need for a subpoena has only recently become apparent. The Chamber will recognise numbers 11 and 12 as names arising from last week's discussion about transcripts. Numbers 9 and 10 are both village witnesses, if I can so describe them, whose disinclination to attend has only recently come to our attention. Number E is a category of those who are simply unwell and, again, not expected to be fit enough necessarily by the end of our case. "F," there are two witnesses. I had them described as "justified unwilling." In each case, a judgement has been made that they should not be subject to further coercive measures. In relation to number 16, the judgement was made by the Tribunal. In relation to number 15, the judgement was made by us; namely, in light of what we were told, it didn't seem appropriate to attempt compulsion. The risks spoken of seemed sufficiently real. Now, number 15 may require further information coming to the Chamber, and it may be that it, in the first instance, in any event, that information should come to the Chamber ex parte, although I wouldn't rule out, as a possibility, the Chamber, having heard what I would have to say about that, would consider the desirability of letting the Defence know. But it's a sensitive matter. What happened, as the Chamber will remember, in relation to number 16, was that the information came ex parte but not from us; it came from another organ of the institution. "G", affidavits, that which we were encouraged from the beginning to use. We've had, of course, huge difficulties with the institutions in Bosnia, getting -- perhaps "cooperation" is the wrong word -- understanding and, to some degree, cooperation. They seemed perhaps reluctant to accommodate us with a procedure that matched what either the letter or the spirit of 94 ter plainly demands. We have, I'm happy to say, we think, been able to achieve what will meet the spirit and, we hope, the letter of 94 ter this week, and so those witnesses, at least numbers 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, and I think 23, probably being seen this week. Number 24, the Chamber will remember, is a witness in respect of whom one piece of evidence was omitted when he was here, and the Chamber took the view that it was inappropriate to require his attendance here simply to produce another exhibit. So that's the menu of -- it looks a bit like a menu too -- the menu of items for the Court to deal with. The matter was argued first by Mr. Lopez-Terres in relation to categories -- well, Category A effectively. There was a skeleton argument submitted by us on the 5th of August of last year, associated with a summary of recent developments on the law of hearsay in Canada, to be of some assistance, if it was, and there was a Defence skeleton argument dated the -- or filed on the 13th of September of 1999, and in truth, I think, those arguments probably set things out fully pretty well on both sides. Obviously we'd like, I'm sure both of us, to have a top-up, as it were, but without exhausting the Chamber. That leaves Category B, which was not forecast in the course of our various references to this general topic in the course of the trial, and it wasn't forecast because it was never known what was going to happen in relation to witness 3. I explained the position in outline last week in order that my friends could not be taken by surprise today, and I was only able to outline the position last week, because it was only then known for the first time that witness 3 was not going to respond to the subpoena that had been issued and that the Chamber took the view that there was no purpose in taking coercive measures further in relation to him. It may be that the best thing to do at the moment would be to ask Mr. Lopez-Terres to deal at some length with Category B, and I ask him to deal with it not only because he's had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The convenient thing, I think, is to deal with these matters one after the other. There is an issue, clearly, on the dead witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That involves one witness whose transcript we have admitted. It may be sensible if we do take the adjournment now and we look at the submissions that have been made in writing about these matters, and then we'll be in a position to deal with at least those two. Different principles may apply in relation to the other matters. Category C -- or "C" we have dealt with. "D," do I take it there are applications for subpoenas?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There are applications in the pipeline, I think, for all of those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Clearly that had better be expedited if they are to give evidence, if there's to be any chance of their giving evidence by the 10th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I respectfully suggest, if the Chamber does take an adjournment, that the statements it may want to look at in order to understand the significance, one way or the other, of the potential witnesses, are number 1, 2, and 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry. The written statements themselves that we are seeking to put in, as the Chamber will appreciate. I wouldn't ask you to look at or cast your eyes over all of them, because they can mostly be dealt with by way of summary, but at some stage the Chamber will need to consider in detail, I suspect, for the purposes of deciding admissibility, the statements concerned, and the ones that I think are most likely to be helpful to read at this stage are the statements of numbers 1, 2, and 15, but I'm told you may not yet have number 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're referring to the numbers of the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I have here the statement of number 2 and the statement of number 1, but not, of course, the statement of number 15. But, as you say, he's in a separate category. But in due course, we should have that. You'll have available the other statements if we need them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll ask Mr. Lopez-Terres, in fact, to deal with both Categories A and B because he started the ball rolling with Category A, and it's only perhaps fair that he should conclude it. We'll hear, of course, any further objections, but my general observations, as we start this topic, are contained in our skeleton argument. I have had prepared, and it may be, if it would help, I can have distributed a short paper dealing with provisions in Germany, Austria, America, Australia, and Japan on these and similar topics, and I think one can perhaps fairly summarise the law from other jurisdictions, in so far as it guides us, by saying that there are generally exceptions in respect of the reading of statements of witnesses who are dead or, for other reasons, unavailable, even where that reading of a statement would either offend a common law rule on hearsay or a civil system principle of morality. They generally are exceptions. The exceptions are variously restricted, sometimes to judicial officers or judges taking the statements -- well, that can't apply here -- sometimes not, and they are frequently, of course, controlled by limitations, whether case law limitations or statutory. But, of course, they are always trying to achieve the balance spoken of between the propriety of the Court having the best possible evidence and the risks associated with the defendant not having the witness there to cross-examine. So the guidance of other jurisdictions may be of interest, and I can certainly make that available this afternoon, but we know that critical features of this Tribunal are that it is professional Judges, that hearsay is, in principle, admissible -- what would otherwise be called hearsay is, in principle, admissible, and that only by having the material available, rather than excluding it altogether, is the Chamber able to put it together with all other evidence, including evidence that may come from the Defence, in due course, to assess its value. For that reason, we would press the Court to say that once every other step has properly been taken to bring the witnesses we wanted to attend here, and we have taken every possible step, why, then, it is appropriate for the Chamber to read the available material coming from that potential witness, in due course, to decide what, if any, weight to attach to it? Finally, before I sit down, I understand that there has been a measure of success in relation to witnesses 6 and 7 -- I'll have to explore that a little more fully after the court rises -- but the Court's coercive powers, which I'm not sure have been used to this extent, or at all, in any other case are seen to be effective. We may have some success with 6 and 7, but I should make the point that in relation to Categories C and D -- or C, D, and E, and F, come to that, I suppose, wherever possible, in the time available, if the affidavit system of "G" does work, then we will also attempt, wherever possible, to obtain affidavits from any of the other witnesses who don't turn up but who have made statements. We would, of course, would argue, and do argue, that their statements should be admissible without the formalities of the affidavit, for the reasons we've already advanced. But just because we must do everything we can to ensure the material in the best condition before the Chamber, we will attempt affidavits for those witnesses as well. So I'll ask Mr. Lopez-Terres to conclude what he has to say about numbers 1 and 2. If the Chamber is happy that we continue by just using numbers for witnesses, then we don't need to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, 2 is already on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to the prior testimony, yes. Oh, the name is, certainly. Yes. Yes. I was only going to propose using numbers because it's so easy to slip up otherwise. But yes, indeed, 2 is on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As far as 2 is concerned, Mr. Friis-Pedersen, there's no difficulty about that. But certainly number 1, if that's thought appropriate, would --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again, as a dead witness, I quite see the point. It hardly even arises, save and so far as he may be linked to a witness who gave evidence under protection. Yes, I'm being artificially and unnecessarily cautious. I'd better sit down before I do something seriously wrong. I'll turn it over to Mr. Lopez-Terres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lopez-Terres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Simply to remind you, to show the framework within which this debate could take place, it goes back to the 15th of June, 1999. For the first time, I asked to admit the testimonies of two witnesses who I'm referring to. On the 16th of June, the Chamber decided that it would admit the statement or the transcript of the evidence of Mr. Friis-Pedersen, that transcript which was made as a deposition in the case of Blaskic, and it was on the 16th of December, 1997, and which reflected one of the counts in the indictment. So that Exhibit 2706, it was already admitted in that case. As for the deposition of Mr. Friis-Pedersen, one of our investigators, on the 24th and 25th of August, 1996, which concerned the testimony of Mr. Haskic on the 13th of September, 1995, and last year, you decided that for the time being, this document was not admissible and that we would have to proffer some other argument, because the initial argument was initially rejected. It was always said in the decision of the 16th of June, 1999 that if the Prosecutor's office still is requesting the admission of this evidence, then we shall hear it, if necessary. So, generally speaking, with regard to the unavailable witnesses and the two dead witnesses that are in this group, they were taken up once again, before the recess in August last year, and today in an agreement which was said or, rather, suggested by your Chamber, on the 16th of June, we once again submitted a motion for the admission of the reports of these two witnesses. The Prosecutor's Office also believes, as regards the first of those witnesses, Mr. Haskic, that his testimony is very -- that his deposition is very important. As for the second statement, the fact that it had already been admitted as evidence in Blaskic's trial does not seem -- it seems sufficient for us to cover all the points that were envisaged by our investigator while he was still alive. So under Rule 90, we wish to tender once again these two testimonies into evidence. If your Chamber does not admit these two statements, still, nevertheless, there is certain information in there which is of interest for us, and we believe that it could be admitted without prejudice, because admission of the truthfulness, after all, and Article -- under Rule 90 of the Rules. We believe that, for evidence of truth, to not to admit the testimony of these two persons would not be fair, because people who died before being able to serve justice should not mean that they should be deprived of the right to be heard or that their testimony be heard by the Chamber, and thus they could also make their contribution to the service of justice, which they were willing to do while they were still alive. These witnesses never indicated that they were not willing to appear before this Chamber. Quite the contrary. According to the transcripts, to the documents that we have, they were both quite willing and available to make their contribution to justice. We do not think that these statements would be -- that this system would be dangerous if this happened in a systematic manner, or that it could be an encouragement for the suppression of some witnesses who could be embarrassing witnesses. Mr. Nice just told you, a couple of moments ago, that in national systems there are rules which envision the admission of testimonies of dead witnesses, and this kind of -- you were informed again of this. In our Rules of Procedure, there are no specific provisions which would take into account that the testimony of witnesses -- of deceased witnesses, but 89(C), on the other hand, does envisage the possibility of admitting that kind of evidence. In your decision on the 29th of July, 1999, that is, the Tulica decision, it was said that the statement or, rather, the record of testimony of witnesses could be admitted, owing to the discretionary powers of the Chamber, and on the basis of all this, we should like to seek the admission of the transcripts of these two statements, of these two transcripts. They're also compatible with the jurisdiction of the European court in Strasbourg, which said that if -- which has refused the declarations coming from deceased persons only if they were the only documents testifying to, but we are not -- in this case, we are not -- this is not the case we have before us here. Mr. Haskic and Mr. Friis-Pedersen were not the only witnesses who would be revealing to this Chamber some information which seems of importance and which I believe should be taken into consideration by the Chamber. As for their demise at the beginning of this argument, there was -- we had some discussions with the Defence. However, their deaths are not in question, because we produce here the death certificates of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. I have the evidence in relation to Mr. Friis-Pedersen before me and the certificate which was introduced from Denmark. I don't have the certificate in relation to the other gentleman. Have you got a copy of it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document is at your disposal. The second witness died on the 4th of July, 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, can I ask you; you referred to the jurisprudence in the European court. Does that jurisprudence, as to the admission of the statements of dead witnesses, make a distinction between statements which are sworn or in relation to which there is a declaration, or does the jurisprudence simply sanction the submission of any statement from a dead witness, leaving it to the Tribunal to determine the weight, or is there any significance attached to -- any requirement that the statement be sworn or that there be some statement as to its truthfulness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, these are statements which could have been taken either by the judicial or by the police authorities. May I add that in some countries, police authorities also can take statements under oath; it is not only the judicial authorities which can do so. As regards the European court, their position is very clear. It says that the admission of such statements as evidence is not incompatible in itself with fairness and under Article 6 of the European Convention. The only limit to this kind of jurisprudence concerns in reminding that in no case may the jurisdiction of the judgement, when it decides to pronounce the guilt of one or another of the accused may be based -- I mean, their conviction may not be based only on such statements, that is, if the accused -- because the accused must be able to provide -- to counterbalance this. So this is the only limit which is imposed. It said that admission of such statements is not, as such, contrary to Article 6 of the convention. I should like to add -- and this is one of the particularities of one of these two statements, that is, one of the Bosniak witness -- that this transcript was already admitted in the Blaskic case on the 29th of April, 1998. And when the Chamber trying this case admitted this transcript as one of the exhibits, it said that this was a transcript which was taken under oath by the investigator from the Prosecutor's Office, and it considered that this also -- I mean, we have the formula on the transcripts which the investigators say -- that is, it is said in the beginning the report and at the end of the statement that such-and-such -- that the declaration of such-and-such a witness is equivalent by the sworn statement, that is, a statement made under oath before the investigator. In the Blaskic case, it was said that this transcript was admitted as an exhibit but that it did not prejudice in any way the weight which this Chamber might put to the information found in those particular transcripts. One thing is to admit it, and another one is, of course, to determine its probative value. It seems all the more important to us, because the information that can be found in these witness statements can naturally be contested as to their credibility by the Defence or by other means, such as the cross-examination. We have already had some experience last week with regard to the discussion about the admission or non-admission of some of the transcripts, and the Defence was able to voice its view regarding the reliability of such evidence, including evidence made under oath before this Tribunal, for instance, a document which was written. So there is no reason why we could not do the same thing with regard to the witness concerned. I'm simply saying that the cross-examination, naturally, is not the only way in which one can test the reliability or the sincerity of certain evidence. For instance, two transcripts of these witnesses are there, and we see no reason to admit one and not to admit the other one. The transcript -- we are seeking again the admission of the Bosnian witness because the Blaskic Chamber admitted it, and this situation is different in this case. But the Chamber in the Blaskic case, therefore, believed that such a transcript was the result of a statement given under oath before an investigator. I hope that I have answered your question. Still discussing this same question of the jurisprudence of the European court, I have indicated that we are not in that situation, because it is quite clear that it is not the intention of the Office of the Prosecutor to require that either of the accused be declared guilty on the basis of these statements. Fortunately, we are not in that situation. That being so, I wish also to say that as regards the statements made by these two witnesses, they have been corroborated and partially completed by other witnesses that have been heard in this Chamber. Therefore, a comparison of these statements which we are asking the acceptance of, and the testimony which your Chamber has already heard, can also be a test and justify the admission of these statements. As regards the substance of these two transcripts and statements, it seems to us quite relevant, as regards the first witness, the Bosniak witness, we know, because the Defence has told us so, that it is contesting the presence of the accused Dario Kordic throughout in the area of Donja Veceriska. This debate was initiated during the testimony of a witness, that is, I think he was Witness V, when he testified about the attack on Veceriska. He was the only witness testifying to those facts. The dead witness tells us several things. He tells us, first, what happened during the evening that preceded the offensive of the 16th of April, 1993, and what he was able to see himself in that village. This village of Veceriska is hardly three kilometres away from Vitez, and during the evening, he noted the presence of the accused Dario Kordic, in uniform, surrounded by bodyguards and participating in festivities, together with other local representatives of the HVO. According to this witness, there were members of the Vitez Brigade there, among whom the local commander of the battalion, named Ivica Drmic, and also there were individuals whose significant signs he recognised -- the Jokers, the Vitezovi -- and he also indicated the presence of a person carrying a badge as member of the Ludvig Pavlovic Brigade, which comes from Herzegovina and which was stationed in the Vitez area in the period we are talking about. The presence of the accused Dario Kordic was testified to. It was also testified that the accused Dario Kordic was in direct contact with the local commander, Ivica Drmic, commander of a battalion of the Vitez Brigade, of which Mario Cerkez was the commander; the witness saying that on several occasions, this battalion commander gave written documents to the accused Dario Kordic. Also, during the evening, he heard these threatening songs about the Muslims disappearing from Veceriska, and then he saw, as indicated by Witness V, who I have already referred to, Croats from the village -- women, children, and elderly people -- who left before the attack was launched. He said that his telephone lines were cut, and later the witness explains, describes in detail the actual attack on his village. For all these reasons, it seemed to us that the information reported by this witness is extremely relevant, extremely useful for an understanding of the facts that occurred in the area of Donja Veceriska in the evening of the 15th of April, and especially the next day, on the 16th, and the following days, because we know the attack continued over several days. This testimony appears to establish a direct link between the accused Dario Kordic and the village in question, the presence of the accused in an area in which the fighting was to occur as of the next day, and by soldiers who we believe, on the basis of evidence, participated in that attack. For all these reasons, it seems to us necessary to admit this report as a relevant piece of evidence, in line with your authority under Rule 89. As regards the second witness, Major Friis-Pedersen, it is true that this witness, as opposed to the first one, had already the opportunity to testify here in the Blaskic case, but during that testimony, this person was examined very succinctly, taking into account the Blaskic case, rather than points that referred to the accused Kordic or Cerkez. Upon reading the transcript and the report -- the statement, rather, given to the investigator in 1996, we see that the witness gave far more information that was not even referred to during his testimony in December 1997, in the course of the Blaskic trial. We wish to recall that Major Friis-Pedersen was a monitor of the European Commission Monitoring Mission, and in that capacity, he went to the area of Central Bosnia from the 26th of January, 1993 until the end of May 1993. Therefore, he had an opportunity to fully inform himself about the environment before the conflict, during the conflict, and on the basis of those elements of information that he gathered as a monitor, in his statement, he was able to refer to events of which he was a witness, or to refer to the conclusions that he himself made. Such information includes, for instance, the fact that when he was in the area, he met Mr. Kordic, in February or March 1993, who was introduced to him as the leading political figure in the region; that he had occasion, on the 16th of April, when the fighting had already broken out, to go to the area of Vitez, to pass close to Ahmici and to see for himself the presence of corpses. He took several photographs, which are attached to his statement. He indicated in his statement that he personally saw HVO soldiers carrying out ethnic cleansing of Muslims -- those are the words he used -- in the village of Bila. He said that he did not have the opportunity, like other ECMM officers, to fully accomplish his tasks that day because HVO snipers were positioned at Gornja Rovna, in the area of Busovaca. He reported visits he made to Vitez with Mario Cerkez, on the 18th and 19th of April, and especially his visit to the Cerkez headquarters, where he saw detainees, Muslims of all ages who were being held there in the basement of the headquarters. He noted, and he stated quite honestly that those prisoners appeared to be well-treated, but in a very limited amount of space, and, as a result, that there were violations of the Geneva Conventions. He participated in a meeting on the 4th of May, 1993 with the British Battalion on the Ahmici massacre, and it was concluded that the attack on that village was part of a coordinated operation for the area around Vitez. He accompanied the witnesses that you also heard here, Mr. McLeod, and in the course of this latest mission, he was comforted by the idea -- he saw that there was a determination by the HVO to prepare an ethnically clear Croat area. All these things were not referred to during his testimony in the Blaskic case in December 1996, and we feel that his statements contain far more detailed information than he was able to provide during the Blaskic trial, and that is why they deserve to be considered by your Chamber. Bearing in mind the explanation I have given, and I apologise for taking a lot of your time, but I wish, on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor, once again, to suggest that the statements of Mr. Haskic, on the 13th of September, 1995, and the statements and reports by Mr. Eric Friis-Pedersen, on the 23rd and 24th of August, 1996, be admitted, together with the photographs attached to those statements, be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I might start out with our view of what the applicable law is. I think there's no dispute, obviously, that the Court is governed by its own Statute and by its Rules in the decision that it makes. With respect to the bench's question about the importance or absence of an oath in the jurisprudence of the European Court of Human Rights, there are a few cases that we would urge the Court to consult. The first would be the Unterpertinger case, decided in 1986, under Austrian law. In this case, a husband beat family members, who then refused to testify, invoking the family privilege. In the trial against the husband, written police statements taken from the family members were permitted to be used. The European Court of Human Rights reversed the ensuing conviction on appeal, under Articles 6(1) and 6(3)(d) of the European Convention on Human Rights, emphasizing the importance of confrontation rights and the absence of any confrontation rights in this case.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Sayers slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Corroboration existed from the police reports, the medical reports, the file on the divorce proceedings, and also the testimony of a sister-in-law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's just pause there. This is a wholly different sort of case. That was a case with a husband and wife, and it was the wife's statement which was admitted. Clearly, a completely crucial witness. In this case, we have had nearly a hundred witnesses, of which, of course, one of these would have been important as a witness; I accept that. But the reason that the European Court took the view that they did was to say, "Well, you cannot found a conviction on such evidence." I mean, that's the ratio, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think that that's accurate, Mr. President. That was the principal evidence against the accused in that case. But I think that the Court needs to take into consideration the legal context in which the decision was made, and I would just recommend, for the Court's consideration as well, a few other cases. The Barbera case from 1988 may be more akin to our case in some ways, in terms of the prominence of the charges made. This was a terrorism case, as I'm sure the Court remembers, and it was a case in which the written statement, unsworn, of an absent witness was introduced into evidence, under Spanish law. The defendants never had an opportunity, in the view of the European Court of Human Rights, to confront or to examine a person whose evidence, which was vital in that case, and had been taken in their absence, and was deemed to be read out at trial. The absence of confrontation led the court, once again, to reverse. Similarly, there are other analogies under the jurisprudence of the European Court of Human Rights. The Bricmont case, the Kostovski case, which was an organised crime case. But one case where a statement was read out, and the court found that this did not violate the rights of the accused, was the Isgrow case, which is representative of that line of cases, I think. But confrontation existed at an early stage of the trial, according to the European Court on Human Rights, because the investigating judge asked questions of the witness, and that constituted the confrontation that Article 6(3)(d) required. Furthermore, corroborative evidence existed in that case, and one other issue was that the defendant actually didn't object contemporaneously to the reading out of that statement, and the waiver issue was discussed too. But that's simply representative, although not determinative, and I would certainly concede that, of the issues before the Court. I think that these two applications have to be treated very differently. They are completely separate. Let me turn to witness 1 first. This issue is significant because this witness has never given any testimony in any of the prior Lasva Valley cases, not in Kupreskic, Aleksovski, Blaskic, or Furundzija, yet the testimony of this witness, according to the Prosecution, is, to use their words, "very important." We would submit to the Court that the testimony that this witness -- or the reason that this witness statement is being offered is on points which are contested as to which there is no other evidence. There is no other witness that puts Mr. Kordic in Donja Veceriska on the night before the attacks in the Lasva Valley, or the fighting in the Lasva Valley. There is no other witness who puts Mr. Kordic in the company of all of the significant military players, if you like, in this story: the Viteska Brigade, the Vitezovi, the Jokers, and the Ludvig Pavlovic Brigade. A very convenient witness to put our client in close proximity to all four units, or members of those units, albeit in a social setting, at a very crucial point in this case, April the 15th, 1993. There is no other evidence to support that contention, and I don't think that the Prosecution tries to contend that there is. In fact, when we heard argument on this issue at an earlier stage, the Prosecutor stood up and represented to the Court that they were going to have corroborative evidence, that there was going to be some sort of evidence of a habit or a pattern on Mr. Kordic's behalf that would be put before the Court, and I'll address that contention in just a minute. But the fundamental point is, without confrontation rights, the only evidence put forward by the Prosecution to establish these contested facts, as far as we are aware, is an unsworn statement -- and it is unsworn -- it hasn't been subjected to cross-examination, in this case, and the witness has never been subjected to cross-examination in any of these cases. It was not contemporaneous, and we would submit it's not reliable. Let me just address a few other issues in connection with this statement, if it please the Court. The first is the death certificate issue. We have finally been provided with a copy of this death certificate, and the cause of the death, I believe, is illegible. The duration of the death is illegible. The doctor's report on the cause of death isn't even filled out, and as far as we can see, it isn't even signed, except with a rubber stamp. The duration of the last illness is absolutely unknown. Whether there were any indications noticed by the family during the course of the illness, which is one of the blanks to be filled out, is left completely blank, not filled out at all. So we do not know how this witness died, the cause of his death, the duration of his illness or, equally important, the state of mind that he was in for the years immediately preceding his illness. We don't know how long he'd been sick. We don't know how long he'd been on medication or if he was on medication. And there are a couple of questions which are left unanswered. If the evidence is so crucial, so important, why was no videotape taken of this gentleman's testimony? Why was no deposition sought or obtained under Rule 71? And why was no affidavit submitted under Rule 94 ter in any of the earlier cases? Let me turn to the subject of the admission of this statement in Blaskic case. It was the Defence that made the motion for the admission of this statement, but, as we've pointed out in our papers, the Defence expressly waived the right to cross-examination of this witness. On page 2 of its submission to the Court, the Blaskic Defence made this contention: "It is only the Defence that can properly object to its admission, on the ground that the Defence was not given an opportunity to cross-examine the declarant. The Defence will waive this objection." Mr. Kordic will not waive the objection. Furthermore, there was no opposition to the admission of this statement from the witness in the Blaskic case by the Prosecutor, and there is ardent opposition to this statement in this case. In Blaskic, I might point out that both sides wanted the statement into evidence for their own reasons. Furthermore, in the decision that was reached by the Blaskic Court, the limited purpose for the admission of the statement was actually underscored by the very Trial Chamber itself. It made this point in its April the 29th, 1998 order, which we've attached as Exhibit B to our papers. The evidence was admitted to establish that Donja Veceriska was a legitimate military target "because it was defended." And as I point out, there is no waiver of the right to cross-examination here. Mr. Kordic contests the factual accuracy of the statements made by this clearly hostile witness, who was on the opposing side of a bitter conflict and in a circumstance where there's no corroboration, no corroborative evidence. Furthermore, we would point out that the statement was made two and a half years after the events in issue. It's not nearly contemporaneous. There's no reference, notes that were made contemporaneously --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, Mr. Sayers, please.
