utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- or any diary that was prepared contemporaneously by the declarant which might otherwise supply some measure of contemporaneous corroboration. Turning to some general principles. Very briefly let me touch upon them. The Prosecutor in this case has used unsworn statements in lieu of live testimony, and we would submit that this deprives the accused of one of the minimum guarantees that he is entitled to, minimum guarantee to a fair trial. One of the components of that is to confront and cross-examine under Article 21(4)(e). So this is a potentially significantly issue, Your Honour. It's not peripheral. And even though this is, as you correctly point out, one of a hundred witnesses, I would respectfully submit that there are no witnesses in this case who have offered such direct, harmful potential testimony about Mr. Kordic's whereabouts on that night. There is no corroboration. Now, on November the 4th, 1999, the Prosecutor said, on page 9541 of the transcript, that: "There is evidence of another witness dealing, in some detail, with sightings of Mr. Kordic at the same place, not on that particular night, but showing a pattern of visits." That's one of the foundations that have been offered up to the Trial Chamber as a justification for admitting this testimony. Witness V testified on November the 25th, 1999, and was asked specifically about the reputation of the declarant, and I think asked by counsel for our co-defendant. This witness, who was related, we believe, to the declarant, said, "I don't know whether he was respected all that much." Page 10403, lines 22 to 23. Furthermore -- and this, I would submit to the Court, is extremely significant -- there was no mention made during the testimony of Witness V in this case, that Witness V, as I've said, we believe to be a relative of the declarant, that Witness V ever had a conversation with the declarant during which the declarant related precisely the same material that's now in his statement to his own relation. Both of these people lived in Donja Veceriska for four years after the fighting was ended. It's a tiny village, to use the words of Witness V. People knew each other. They talked. But there's no mention in Witness V's testimony of any kind of corroboration whatsoever of the specific sightings to which Mr. Kordic objects, as a matter of principle and as a matter of fact. In fact, Witness V said he saw Mr. Kordic once at the cafe owned by Franjo Drmic. That's at page 10396 of the transcript. And one visit does not a habit make, as the Court well knows. So for all of those reasons, we object vigorously to the introduction of the witness statement of this witness, which is not sworn, which was not given under oath, which is contested, and which is the own evidence on that particular point. Now, turning to the second witness, my argument is going to be extremely short with respect to that. His testimony from the Blaskic case is already in evidence. It was given on December the 16th, 1997, and it's been introduced as Exhibit Z2706. It was introduced under the rationale of Aleksovski. And why? We stood up before the Court and represented to the Court that we could not in good conscience say that we could have expected to have elicited from this witness anything more by way of cross-examination than was elicited by Defence counsel in that case. Now, not content with that, apparently, the Prosecution also wants his unsworn witness statement of August the 23rd and 24th, 1996 introduced. Well, that's a different category altogether. The Blaskic Prosecutor had every incentive and every reason to ask all relevant questions of this witness. The Court's already stated that, with respect to the matters at issue, the core set of events, there's something of an identity of interest between the defendant in the Blaskic case and the defendants in this case, and that's probably right with respect to the historical facts. But the witness statement here is cumulative. It's unnecessary. The reason that it's cumulative and unnecessary is just consider the ECMM witnesses who have already covered this area: Mr. McLeod, Major Baggesen, Mr. Lawson, Colonel Morsink, Colonel Weckesser, Major Jennings, Major Bower -- well, these are BritBat witnesses -- Major Jennings, Major Bower, and Major Buffini, and then there's another witness, Colonel Landry, who's going to cover this same territory. So there's no necessity for this witness statement at all. But the narrowest and easiest point upon which the Court's decision could and should be made, we would suspect, is merely an application of the Tulica decision, page 10, paragraph 26, where the Court considered the admission of a transcript of a witness testimony of someone who's already given evidence, and the Court said: "The inclusion of this material is unnecessary, repetitious, as it already forms part of the record in this trial, and the transcript of Witness N, as part of the dossier, is, accordingly, not admitted." Same here. You already have the gentleman's testimony, the Major's testimony, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, could you slow down, please. Could counsel slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- should not be admitted. It's cumulative. Now, with respect to the other witnesses, I only have just a few observations to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going to deal with these witnesses first.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] To begin with, I fully agree with the argument proffered by my learned friend, Mr. Sayers. In order to avoid repetition, I should like to say only two or three things more to round off the picture. There is evidently a major difference between the use of the record of the statement -- of the transcript of the evidence of a witness given in a different case, not only because it was done under oath but because it was not made before the Court, especially this Court. The situation is completely different when this comes to statements made to investigators, whether investigators of this Tribunal or investigators of domestic or international authorities of another nature. When we speak about witnesses 1 and 2, I think this whole matter has, rather deliberately or not, but been obfuscated to a point. The only way is to admit the statement given to investigators. That is case one. And as was done in the Blaskic case, the only ground for that can be an understanding between the two parties. That is, if the Defence waives the right which is otherwise not under question, if the Defence waives his right to cross-examine the witness, and here we are not ready to waive that right, and as the witness, unfortunately, is dead, the witness will not be able to appear before this Court. Another thing I wanted to say, and my colleague has just reminded us of the standard laid down by this Chamber in the Tulica decision, something else I wanted to say, and that has to do with the European Court in Strasbourg. I do not think that that particular standard -- I think that that particular standard needs to be considered with a grain of salt, because the court in Strasbourg and its rules address human rights, whereas this Tribunal addresses mostly individual criminal responsibility. And we all know that this is not one and the same thing, and we, therefore, can conclude that the standard of proving need not be the same, because in all legal systems, it is the criminal proceedings which require the highest possible standards. I presume you do not expect me to address the matter of other witnesses, because we are now addressing only witnesses 1 and 2, and this, perhaps, would be all that I have to say at this point, except perhaps another suggestion, which at first glance may seem strange, but I will say it nevertheless. The Prosecutor, in case he does not manage to persuade the Chamber to admit the first witness's testimony, the Prosecutor, just in case, recounted the statement of that witness as he sees it. I think this is contamination of this transcript. When one goes back to that transcript in nine or ten years' time, I think it would be best to exclude that part of the statement, because the recounting of the statement of this witness means, in a way, producing the testimony on behalf of that witness, and I am again referring to witnesses 1 and 2. So I think it should be excluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, you need not trouble about that. What counsel says from his place is not evidence. It's merely recounting what's in a witness statement. Therefore, as far as we're concerned, it's no more than what we've read in the witness statement. As far as anybody who comes to read the transcript is concerned, they must understand that too. It's merely a submission by counsel, and nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, Mr. President, only a few comments after what has been said. I remind that in the decision of the Blaskic Chamber, on the 29th of April, 1998, it was clearly said in the decision that the statement of the Bosnian witness, who is dead, who died of natural causes, that his statement was made under oath to the investigators of the Prosecution. Considering that this admission does not prejudice the opinion of the Chamber regarding the admission of the Defence, according to which this statement might establish that the place of Veceriska, Donja Veceriska, was a legitimate military target and that that was why it was defended. The Chamber reserves the right to determine the probative value of that particular piece of evidence. The Blaskic Chamber, naturally, admitted it, made the reservation, and they said that, aside from admitting a document, it would then assess the probative value of that document. The Chamber also considered that that statement taken in 1995 was made under oath. I'm quite sure, at this point, that at this Tribunal we do not have an investigating Judge who could take such statements under oath, as is the case in some European legal systems. However, Article 18 of the Statute of this Tribunal indicates that the Prosecutor's Office, at least in the French version of the document, is responsible for the investigation and for interviews. The investigators are not Investigating Magistrates. They do not form the Investigating Judges who will be taking statements under oath. In European systems, it is mentioned, however, but nevertheless, when a witness makes a statement to us, he takes it upon himself to tell the truth and what they have lived or seen or heard. And it is indicated that they heard something from third parties, but nevertheless, when they make a statement, then they take it upon themselves to tell the truth. We do not have here a system of Investigating Judges, and therefore our investigators take these statements in the manner in which it is done here, and I've already described that. The investigator who took a statement, of course, the investigator who took the statement of this witness could also be called if this becomes -- if this is necessary. Mr. Sayers said that it was not the practice of the Prosecutor's Office to make video-conferences, but in 1995 there was no reason -- Mr. Sayers speaks about the videotape, but in 1995, simply nobody thought that it would be necessary to video Mr. Haskic's interview. Unfortunately, he died on the 4th of June, 1997, at the moment when the Blaskic -- and there was no reason at that particular time to think that that particular statement should be videoed or recorded in any way. There was no reason in 1995 why this witness, at the time when this witness was giving his statement, whether his health was precarious or whether something would happen, and that is simply why I did not get anyone to request from this witness a health certificate or anything like that during the procedure. Finally, I should like to say, with regard to this testimony or, rather, the record of this testimony, that the testimony of Midhat Haskic's must have been considered sufficiently reliable by the Defence there, because they requested that it be admitted into evidence. When one reads that statement, one sees that Mr. Haskic indeed reveals what happened in his village, what happened during the attack, and clearly explains that the villagers were defending themselves fiercely when they were attacked, and this evidence, it seems to us, is quite straightforward. Unfortunately, the witness died, but, as I have said a few moments ago, we nevertheless believe that it should be another contribution to justice, as he would have done had he lived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is an application by the Prosecution to admit the witness statements of two witnesses who, since they've made their statements, have died. Mr. Haskic made a statement in September of 1995, and died in June 1997. The Prosecutor applies to admit the statement under Rule 89(C), which permits the Chamber to admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value, but, of course, Rule 90 says that witnesses shall, in principle, be heard directly by the Chambers. The Prosecution say that this is an exception, of course, the witness being dead and, therefore, his direct evidence not being available. They rely upon the jurisprudence of the European Court of Human Rights, which has held that such evidence does not necessarily contravene Article 6, and they refer to the Isgrow case, amongst others. But, of course, in Unterpringer, the court said that there may be such a violation, and a conviction quashed, if it is the sole basis for conviction. It is accepted that Mr. Haskic dealt, in his statement, with an important issue relating to the accused Dario Kordic, his presence in Donja Veceriska on the evening of the 15th of April, 1993, when he was in company with members of the military. The Defence object partly on that ground. They say that it means that important evidence is not cross-examined, and there is, therefore, an absence of confrontation of such evidence. They also say that the death certificate contains blanks. Well, that by itself would not be sufficient not to include the evidence, unless we were satisfied that it was, in some way, not authentic, which we are not. The Prosecution rely on the fact that this evidence was admitted in the Blaskic trial, but the Defence, with some justification, point out that in that case, it was at the application of the Defence that the statement was admitted and there was no objection, and therefore circumstances here are different. And the Defence are right about that. The real issue is this: Should this statement be admitted un-cross-examined, so that the Defence have had no chance to test it, we have come to the conclusion that it would be wrong to deny the Chamber this statement simply on that technical ground. That goes very much to the matter of weight. There is a discretion to admit the evidence under 89(C), and we do so, it being of course understood that this is evidence, when we come to consider it, first of all, which, we will have to bear in mind, was not subject to cross-examination and, therefore, lacks that important support. It was not given under oath, although there was an acknowledgement made, which is attached to the statement, which says quite plainly that the maker made the statement voluntarily, being aware that it may be used in legal proceedings. Nonetheless, it was not given under oath. Those are matters which we bear in mind. We shall also, of course, have in mind this, as the European Court has pointed out: that it would not be possible to convict the accused on the basis of this statement alone if that evidence was uncorroborated, and that is a matter which we shall also have in mind. Turning to the evidence of the second statement, different considerations apply. The transcript of his evidence has already been admitted. As we said in Tulica, we did not there admit witness statements where transcripts had been admitted, and we think it right to be consistent in this case. There is not sufficient additional evidence given in this statement to make it right to admit it when the transcript has already been given. What there is is cumulative; it's already been dealt with by a number of other witnesses. For those reasons, we shall not admit the statement of Mr. Friis-Pedersen, but we shall admit that of Mr. Haskic. That leaves other matters which it may be convenient to deal with tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. Obviously, Category B may take a little time to deal with, but I think the others are pretty well generic, with the possible exception of, I don't know, 15 and 16. As to 15, as I've said earlier, there is information available to me at the moment, in a form that I would rather deal with ex parte, about his unwillingness. I know on a previous occasion the Chamber was very concerned about how that information should be communicated to the Court. It's not easy, or really possible, I think, for the Victims and Witnesses Unit themselves to obtain an account from the person, certainly not at short notice, possibly at all. It could be dealt with in writing by our side, in the first instance, if that would be acceptable, and we could launch something along with the statement before tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. If it's put in that form, we will consider it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, what is the programme for tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It seems to me it would be prudent to press on with these as quickly as we can, and then to deal with the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres confirms that the agreement between the parties has been only limited, and then I think enough has been spent on that exercise and we must simply get on and produce the map to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we'll deal with the other matters of admission of evidence, and then we'll deal with the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: And the tapes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, and the tapes too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour. There is also an application that we would make relating to the maps. I know that the Court has asked for the presentation of maps containing depictions of the front lines, and that would be helpful. But we would submit that the report that was prepared by Mr. Elford goes beyond merely that exercise, and there's an issue relating to that which we would like to bring to the Court's preliminary attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Before the map-giver gives evidence, we will decide what he can give evidence about and what he can't. Half past nine, then, tomorrow morning, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
